column4: Humiliation and الْمَسْكَنَةُ are struck upon a people; this is the Quranic form of the section's named masqanah sense, where miskīn carries abasement and weakness as well as poverty.
The repeated pairing of abasement with الْمَسْكَنَةُ confirms the named root-sense of a lowly condition imposed upon a body and community.
The punishment has no دَافِعٍ, using the source section's dictionary-gloss root دفع shortly before 52:13 depicts the guilty themselves being violently pushed.
Punishment for the disbelievers has no repeller, repeating the dictionary-gloss sense of دفع and marking the final limit of any protective interposition.
The condemned people did not restrain one another from wrongdoing; reciprocal moral prompting fails here just as mutual urging toward the poor person's food fails in the section.
The prisoners add that they denied the Day of Judgment, completing the sequence of neglected prayer and neglected feeding in 74:43-44 and matching the stance behind surah 107's acts.
The question points to a person who actively forbids another, staging a human barrier whose target is identified as a praying servant in 96:10.
The person obstructed in the preceding ayah is at prayer, joining bodily interposition to worship rather than to food or a useful object.
A vulnerable community asks for a barrier against people who corrupt the land, explicitly seeking the protective face of interposition developed in the section.
The ruler promises to place a rampart between the community and its attackers, making a wall serve exposed people rather than exclude them from provision.
The attackers can neither scale nor pierce the barrier, showing what an effective protective enclosure does for the people behind it.
An ant warns the other ants to enter their dwellings so that stronger bodies do not crush them; the س ك ن dwelling-root, communal urging, shelter, and vulnerable bodies meet in one scene.
A debtor in hardship must be given time until ease, and remission is better; the creditor is told to lift pressure from a need-stopped person rather than push him further down.
Poor emigrants have been driven from homes and property; their forced bodily expulsion gives a communal scale to the orphan's shove from safety and goods.
Weak men, women, and children who lack power and cannot find a way embody vulnerability as literal inability to move themselves out of danger.
Those who mock believers able to give only their effort add social injury to poverty; God's answering judgment turns contempt back upon the mockers.
The Prophet is told to keep himself with humble worshipers and not let his eyes pass beyond them toward worldly adornment, reversing elite-driven social exclusion.
The elite call Noah's followers the lowest people, identifying the contempt that generates the pressure he refuses in 26:114 to drive believers away.
Noah's chiefs dismiss his visible followers as society's lowest, supplying the status judgment behind his refusal in 11:29 to expel them.
The privileged ask contemptuously whether these vulnerable believers are the ones God favored, continuing the social test surrounding the ban on driving them away in 6:52.
Fear of failing justice toward orphans governs what adults may do in marriage, extending the protective duty to orphaned women exposed to a guardian's power.
Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminders or injury preserve the recipient's body and dignity from a second, social kind of shove.
Whoever makes a good intercession receives a share in it; a single mediating word can move another person toward good, the minimum action absent from the section's man.
The question of who could provide if God withheld provision exposes human dependence even as people presume to withhold small means from someone more visibly dependent.
No one can withhold mercy God opens or release what He withholds, setting human obstruction of aid inside the absolute boundary of divine provision.
The most balanced garden owner says he had urged the others to glorify God, preserving within the exclusion story the possibility and responsibility of one corrective voice.
The person who never urged care for the poor now has no intimate friend, making the lost human circle a consequence of refusing to activate that circle for another.
In abundance the person calls wealth divine honor; paired with 89:16, this false measure is corrected by the ensuing test of how the orphan and poor are treated.
Noah's son imagines a mountain can protect him, but no protector exists against God's decree; a literal high barrier proves unable to supply the saving enclosure he seeks.
Believers are told to protect themselves and their families from fire, giving human authority the positive task of forming a protective circle around dependent bodies.
God saves people from the brink of a fire-pit and makes former enemies brothers, joining rescue from a fall with creation of a supporting human circle.
People are called to spend, yet some withhold; the ayah says the withholder withholds only against himself, returning the obstruction to its maker.
The commands to heed, obey, and spend are followed by protection from one's own stinginess, locating the barrier first within the person whose hand must open.
Satan threatens poverty and commands indecency, supplying the counter-voice that drives people away from giving while God promises bounty and forgiveness.
God asks Iblis what مَنَعَكَ from prostrating; the named root here marks arrogance as an inward barrier stopping a commanded bodily lowering.
The repeated question about what prevented prostration again gives م ن ع an inward sense: self-exaltation arrests a body before worship.
God makes houses a سَكَنًا, turning the section's stillness-root into physical shelter and repose rather than abandonment or incapacity.
The blind, disabled, and sick are explicitly freed from blame around eating in households, dismantling social barriers that could leave vulnerable bodies outside shared food.
Feeding a poor person is made a concrete compensatory obligation in fasting, giving طَعَامُ مِسْكِينٍ a measured legal form rather than leaving it to optional impulse.
Feeding ten poor people from the ordinary food of one's household makes the poor person's food a specified duty in expiation.
Feeding sixty poor people is the required expiation when other means are unavailable, another concrete obligation to move food toward need.
Sacrificial provision is explicitly to be eaten and fed to the afflicted poor person, directing a public rite outward toward hunger.
The command to feed both the contented and the petitioner turns sacrificial worship into food shared across the social boundary of asking.
Mandatory alms are assigned to the poor and needy among named recipients, institutionally removing the giver's option to wall off the whole provision.
A fixed share of communal gains belongs to orphans and the needy, placing weak bodies inside the distribution before individual hands can exclude them.
The God-fearing are also conducted in groups, but toward an opened garden and greeting of peace; paired with 39:71, it bounds the degrading force of herd-like movement by destination and reception.
Believers who approach are to be received with peace and assurance of mercy, the welcoming speech that answers the nearby temptation to drive vulnerable worshipers away.
Prophetic gentleness keeps people gathered, while harshness would make them disperse; the ayah shows how a leader's manner either preserves or breaks the human circle.
Lowering the wing of humility and mercy to aging parents gives strength a bodily posture that shelters weakness instead of bearing down upon it.
The Prophet is told to lower his wing to believing followers, a protective downward posture opposite the raised, pushing hand of social superiority.
The repeated command to lower the wing to believers makes leadership bend toward its people rather than thrust them away for worldly status.
Those who command righteousness while forgetting themselves establish the opposite boundary: exhorting speech alone can also be empty when the speaker's own body does not follow.
The weak, sick, and those without means are released from an obligation they cannot physically meet when they remain sincere, distinguishing inability from culpable moral stillness.
A person whose provision is restricted spends from what God has given, and God promises ease after hardship; constriction calibrates duty without making need a mark of humiliation.
